opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something right in it, but I'd put it differently. It's true that, by themselves, these models don't hand us an explanation. You train a huge network on a huge amount of text, it works remarkably well, and at the end you still don't know *why* it works. In that sense it's more like having built a new kind of object than having understood something. So I agree with Chomsky that the success alone isn't the science.

Where I disagree is the conclusion that there's nothing scientific to take from it. To me these models are fantastic *objects of study*. Think about the history of physics: the steam engine came before thermodynamics, and the steam engine was "just technology," but trying to understand why it worked, and what limited its efficiency, led to some of the deepest ideas we have. I think we're in a similar situation. We have systems that learn the structure of language, or images, from data, apparently beating the curse of dimensionality, and we don't have a theory for that. That's a scientific question, and a very good one.

And it touches on Chomsky's own concerns. His classic argument is about the poverty of the stimulus: children can't learn grammar from the data they receive, so much of it must be innate. Language models don't settle that directly, because they see vastly more data than a child. But they let us ask quantitative questions we couldn't ask before. How much data do you actually need to learn a hierarchical, compositional structure? How does that number scale with the depth of the hierarchy, or with the vocabulary? Which structure is learned first, local correlations then longer-range ones? In my group we study this with synthetic models of data, simple generative grammars with hierarchical structure, where you can compute things and see how sample complexity relates to the structure of the data. That's how you turn a technological achievement into understanding.

So I'd say: Chomsky is right that a working machine is not a theory. But the machine raises very sharp questions, and answering them is science, possibly even science that eventually informs his debate about what is innate and what is learned.

r001.rationale: It describes models learning language structure as an observed capability without a theory, and calls explaining that capability a scientific question.

r002.rationale: It asks how models learn hierarchical and compositional structure, but does not propose investigating how that structure is encoded in artificial neurons.

r003.rationale: It presents these models as worthwhile objects of scientific study in their own right, without making that value depend on explaining biological intelligence.

r004.rationale: It compares language models to the steam engine: a technological development that preceded thermodynamics and prompted scientific questions about how it worked and its limits.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Chomsky is half right, and the half he gets wrong is the interesting part.

He's right that a trained network is not a theory. If you hand me a trillion parameters, I have not learned anything about language in the way that a grammar or a phonological rule tells me something. The model predicts, it does not explain. And he's right that this is how engineering usually works: you get something that functions long before you understand why.

But that's exactly where I'd push back, because historically that gap is where science comes from. The steam engine preceded thermodynamics. People built engines that worked, and then Carnot asked why some were more efficient than others, and out of that came entropy, one of the deepest concepts in physics. The engine was not the science. The engine was the phenomenon that made the science necessary.

I think we're in that moment with deep learning. We have an object that does something we did not expect. It learns from high-dimensional data, in situations where every classical argument about the curse of dimensionality says it should fail, and it doesn't. It generalizes with far fewer examples than the naive count would suggest. Why? That is a genuine scientific question. It's not a question about engineering, it's a question about the structure of the data and the structure of the learning process, and my own view, coming from physics, is that the answer has to do with the fact that natural data are compositional and hierarchical. Low-level features combine into intermediate ones, which combine into higher ones, and a deep network can exploit that structure in a way a shallow method cannot. You can actually make this precise with toy models of hierarchical data, compute how many samples you need, and see the same scaling laws appear that people observe empirically.

So where I'd disagree with Chomsky is in treating the models as the end point. They're the experimental system. The way a physicist studies a magnet or a glass, we can study these networks: measure how performance scales, perturb them, build simplified models that reproduce the behavior, and ask what minimal ingredients are needed. That is science, and it is science about a question his own field cares about, which is how it's possible to learn structure from finite data at all.

Where I'd agree with him is that this hasn't happened yet at the level he would want. We have a growing theory of learning in these systems, but we don't have a theory of language that comes out of them. Whether that's possible, I honestly don't know. But saying the achievement is "merely" technological is a bit like saying a telescope is merely an achievement in glass grinding. It is, and then you point it at the sky.

r001.rationale: It describes deep learning’s unexpected generalization as an observed phenomenon and asks why it happens, calling this a genuine scientific question.

r002.rationale: It discusses studying networks and their learning behavior, but does not propose investigating how they encode linguistic structure in artificial neurons.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that machine intelligence is interesting independently of whether it explains biological intelligence.

r004.rationale: It compares deep learning to the steam engine that preceded Carnot’s work, framing the technology as a phenomenon that makes scientific questions necessary.

astra-6.text:
I think that distinction is too sharp. You can build something for technological reasons and still create a very interesting scientific problem. With large language models, we have systems that acquire remarkable capabilities through training, and we don’t fully understand how those capabilities emerge. That is something science can investigate.

Now, does building a successful language model mean that you have explained human language? No. A system can produce similar behavior through a different mechanism. So I would distinguish demonstrating what learning can achieve from explaining how a child learns.

But these models can still challenge our intuitions about what requires an innate structure and what can be learned from data. They don’t settle that question, particularly because their training conditions are so different from those of humans. What they give us is a new way to ask it. The scientific contribution comes from turning those observations into explanations and predictions that we can test.

r001.rationale: It describes remarkable capabilities acquired through training, says their emergence is not fully understood, and presents that as something science can investigate.

r002.rationale: It does not propose investigating how linguistic structure is encoded in artificial neurons.

r003.rationale: It calls these systems scientifically interesting and distinguishes studying what machine learning can achieve from explaining how a child learns.

r004.rationale: It makes no analogy to Carnot or to technological developments generating questions for physics.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate two questions. One is whether building a large language model, by itself, gives us a scientific explanation of language. Clearly, producing something that works is not the same as understanding why it works. In that sense, I have some sympathy with the distinction Chomsky is making.

But the stronger claim—that these models contribute nothing to science—seems much harder to defend. If a system learns complex linguistic behavior from a relatively simple training objective, that is an interesting observation. It constrains what we can say about learning and about which ingredients are necessary for that behavior. It doesn’t establish that the brain works in the same way, but it gives us something to investigate.

From a physics perspective, these systems also pose scientific questions: Why do they generalize? Which properties of the data matter? Why do certain capabilities appear as you increase the size? We can try to develop theories and test them against experiments.

So I wouldn’t identify technological success with scientific understanding. But I wouldn’t put a wall between them either. You can build something before you understand it, and then the effort to understand it becomes science.

r001.rationale: It calls learned linguistic behavior an interesting observation and raises questions about learning, generalization, data, and emerging capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not propose investigating how linguistic structure is encoded in artificial neurons.

r003.rationale: It says the models raise scientific questions and may not work like the brain, but does not clearly argue that machine intelligence is interesting independently of explaining biological intelligence.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Carnot or draw an analogy to technology prompting questions for physics.
